title: Cargo liquefaction: why Group A bulk cargo flows and what the TML means

scenes.label: CARGO HAZARD
scenes.heading: Dry on the quay. Liquid at sea. Why?
scenes.narration: The ore looked dry on the quay. Three days out, it moves like a liquid and your bulk carrier takes a list. Why?

scenes.label: THE SITUATION
scenes.heading: Iron ore fines: IMSBC Group A
scenes.narration: You are the Chief Officer loading iron ore fines: a Group A cargo under the IMSBC Code, one that may liquefy.

scenes.label: HOW IT HAPPENS
scenes.heading: Motion squeezes water up: slurry
scenes.narration: The ship's motion compacts the fine particles. Water is squeezed up between the grains, and the cargo becomes a slurry that flows to one side.

scenes.label: THE LIMIT
scenes.heading: TML = 90% of the flow moisture point
scenes.narration: So each cargo has a transportable moisture limit, the TML. From a flow table test, it is 90 percent of the flow moisture point.

scenes.label: WHILE LOADING
scenes.heading: Check the paper, then test the cargo
scenes.narration: Before loading: TML certificate under six months old, moisture tested within seven days. During loading, can tests. Free water on the sample? Stop and get lab results.

scenes.label: COMMON MISTAKE
scenes.heading: A passed can test proves nothing
scenes.narration: The common mistake: trusting a passed can test. It is only a rough check. It never proves the moisture is below the TML.

scenes.label: KEY TAKEAWAY
scenes.heading: Certificates first, can tests always
scenes.narration: Certificates first, can tests always, and never load above the TML.

sources.title: Beware cargoes which may liquefy not listed in the IMSBC Code

factCheck.notes: Swedish Club: Group A cargoes (e.g. iron ore fines, nickel ore, mineral concentrates) may liquefy if shipped above their TML; liquefaction = cargo turns from solid to an almost fluid state as the ship moves. TML: for the flow table and penetration tests, 90% of the flow moisture point (other test methods differ - script says 'from a flow table test'). TML certificate no older than six months; moisture sampling/testing never more than seven days before loading; can test is not quantitative, only indicates whether the FMP may be exceeded, must not be relied on alone; free moisture on the sample - arrange laboratory tests, reject/stop until results show moisture below TML. Mechanism (compaction by ship motion, water pressure between particles rises) is the standard explanation. 'Three days out' is an illustrative scenario, not a real casualty. Exact time limits can vary for cargoes with specific schedule provisions: script follows the general IMSBC rule.
